steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: Add the import statement at the top of your TypeScript file.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have the necessary imports to use React and state in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've imported React and useState correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named FormComponent that returns JSX. The component should be empty for now (return null).
steps.hint: Define a function or arrow function named FormComponent that returns null.
steps.seedCode:
// Import React and useState from 'react'

// Create the FormComponent functional component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A FormComponent function is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: FormComponent is defined as a functional component and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the FormComponent functional component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but make sure it's named exactly FormComponent and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating a functional component named FormComponent that returns null.

steps.title: Initialize form state
steps.instruction: Inside your FormComponent, use useState to initialize a state variable named 'formData'. Type it as an object with 'name' and 'email' fields, both strings, and initialize both to empty strings.
steps.hint: Remember to use the useState hook you imported. The type can be defined inline: useState<{name: string, email: string}>({name: '', email: ''}).
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: typed state initialization
const [user, setUser] = useState<{username: string, age: number}>({username: '', age: 0});
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a typed formData state variable initialized with empty name and email fields.
successCriteria: formData state is declared with useState, typed as an object with name and email string properties, and initialized with empty strings for both.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've correctly initialized a typed formData state object.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure formData is typed as an object with both name and email as strings, and both are initialized to empty strings.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Use useState to create a state variable named formData with the correct TypeScript type and initial values.

steps.title: Define the form submit handler type
steps.instruction: Inside the FormComponent, define a handleSubmit function that takes a React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> parameter and returns void. For now, just prevent the default form submission behavior inside it.
steps.hint: Create a function that accepts an event parameter typed as React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> and calls event.preventDefault() to stop the page from refreshing.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a typed handleSubmit function ready to be connected to a form's onSubmit event.
successCriteria: The handleSubmit function is defined with the correct parameter type and prevents default form submission.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've properly typed the form submit event handler with React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but check the parameter type or the preventDefault call.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSubmit function is missing or has incorrect typing.

steps.title: Create the form submit handler
steps.instruction: Inside the FormComponent, implement the handleSubmit function that takes a React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> parameter, calls preventDefault on the event, and logs the current formData state to the console.
steps.hint: Define the function with the correct parameter type annotation. Inside the function body, call event.preventDefault() and then console.log(formData).
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleSubmit function is defined with proper TypeScript typing and logs the formData when called.
successCriteria: handleSubmit function is defined with React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement> parameter, calls event.preventDefault(), and logs formData to console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the typed form submit handler.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your handleSubmit function has the correct parameter type, calls preventDefault, and logs formData.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleSubmit function isn't implemented correctly. Check the parameter type and function body.

steps.title: Add the form element
steps.instruction: Return a form element from your component with an onSubmit handler wired to handleSubmit.
steps.hint: Replace the current return statement (return null) with a form element that uses the onSubmit prop.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns a form element with the handleSubmit function attached to its onSubmit event.
successCriteria: The component returns a form element with an onSubmit handler that calls handleSubmit.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the form element with the correct submit handler.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning a form element with onSubmit={handleSubmit}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The form element or its onSubmit handler is missing or incorrect.

steps.title: Add name input field
steps.instruction: Inside the form element, add an input field for the user's name. Set its type to 'text', bind its value to formData.name, and add an onChange handler to update the state when the user types.
steps.hint: Create a controlled input by setting value={formData.name} and onChange={(e) => setFormData({...formData, name: e.target.value})}.
steps.analogousExample:
// Controlled input example
<input type="text" value={someState} onChange={(e) => setSomeState(e.target.value)} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The form should now include a text input for the name, with its value controlled by the formData state.
successCriteria: An input element with type='text', value={formData.name}, and an onChange handler that updates formData.name is added inside the form.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a controlled input for the name field. The input's value is now bound to the formData state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an input, but it might be missing the value binding or onChange handler. Make sure it's fully controlled by the formData state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The name input field is not correctly implemented. Ensure you have an input element with type='text', value={formData.name}, and an onChange handler that updates the state.

steps.title: Add email input field
steps.instruction: Add an email input field inside the form, below the name input. Bind its value to formData.email and add an onChange handler that updates the email property in formData.
steps.hint: Create an input element with type='email', value={formData.email}, and onChange={(e) => setFormData({...formData, email: e.target.value})}.
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will have two input fields: one for name and one for email. The email input will be properly typed and update the formData state when changed.
successCriteria: An email input field is added with type='email', value bound to formData.email, and an onChange handler that updates the email property in formData.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the email input field with proper TypeScript typing and state binding.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an email input, but check that it has the correct type attribute, value binding, and onChange handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The email input field is missing or incomplete. Make sure to add an input element with type='email', value={formData.email}, and an onChange handler.

steps.title: Add submit button
steps.instruction: Add a submit button inside the form element to allow users to submit the form.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with type="submit" attribute to create a submit button.
steps.analogousExample:
// Adding a submit button to a form
<form>
  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>
steps.expectedOutcome: A submit button appears inside the form element, allowing users to trigger the form submission.
successCriteria: The form contains a <button> element with type="submit" attribute.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a submit button to complete the form.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a button with type="submit" inside the form.
steps.feedbackWrong: The submit button is missing or incorrect. Add a <button type="submit"> inside the form element.

steps.title: Display submitted data
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element below the form to display the current formData values. The paragraph should show both the name and email values.
steps.hint: Place the paragraph after the closing </form> tag. Use JSX curly braces to embed the formData values.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying state values in a paragraph

Name: {formData.name}, Email: {formData.email}
steps.expectedOutcome: The form will now show a paragraph below it displaying the current name and email values from formData.
successCriteria: A paragraph element exists below the form that displays both formData.name and formData.email values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a paragraph to display the form data values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a paragraph, but make sure it displays both the name and email values from formData.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element is missing or doesn't display the formData values correctly.
